Expectation1: Maintain regular communication with family members
Situation1: The grandparent learns that a family member is dealing with a significant personal crisis.
Situation2: They notice a minor ethical dilemma at work, like someone cutting in line, and feel a mild urge to act.
Story:
This morning, my phone buzzed with a message from my daughter. She sounded worried—her husband had lost his job, and she needed someone to talk to. As a grandparent, I know how important it is to be present, to offer comfort and guidance, especially when the family is in distress. I promised myself I would call her during my lunch break. 

But as I stood in the cafeteria line at work, I saw a colleague quietly slip ahead of others. It was a small act, but as a Hindu, I am taught to uphold dharma, to act with honesty and fairness, even in the smallest matters. My conscience pricked me, urging me to speak up, to gently remind my colleague of the right thing to do. Yet, my phone vibrated again—a reminder to call my daughter. I felt torn, pulled between my duty to my family and my responsibility to uphold my ethical values at work. My heart raced as I weighed which role needed me more in that moment.
